Calculus · Part II · Derivatives

Module 5Rules of differentiation

Differentiate products, quotients, trigonometric functions and compositions by rule instead of by limit, know why each rule is true, and check your answers by hand, on a graph and with SymPy. You will also see how a program differentiates another program exactly, with dual numbers.

⏱ 255 minYou need: Modules 1 to 4, in particular the derivative and its first rules (Module 4)

In this module you will

  • Prove and use the product and quotient rules, and extend the power rule to negative integers
  • Differentiate the six trigonometric functions, starting from the limits of Module 2
  • Recognise a composition and differentiate it with the chain rule, through chains of any length
  • Combine the rules systematically, and simplify and check the results
  • Use SymPy to differentiate, and decide whether two different-looking answers are equal
  • Explain how automatic differentiation with dual numbers computes exact derivatives
1

Building derivatives from pieces

Module 4 defined the derivative of a function fff at xxx as a limit,

f′(x)=lim⁡h→0f(x+h)−f(x)h,f'(x) = \lim_{h\to0}\frac{f(x + h) - f(x)}{h},f′(x)=h→0lim​hf(x+h)−f(x)​,

and worked it out for the simplest functions: a constant has derivative 0, and ddxxn=nxn−1\dfrac{d}{dx}x^n = nx^{n-1}dxd​xn=nxn−1 for every positive integer nnn (the power rule). It also proved two rules that build new derivatives from old ones: the derivative of a sum or a difference is the sum or difference of the derivatives, (f±g)′=f′±g′,(f \pm g)' = f' \pm g'\mathclose{\text{,}}(f±g)′=f′±g′, and a constant factor stays where it is, (cf)′=cf′.(cf)' = cf'\mathclose{\text{.}}(cf)′=cf′. With these, every polynomial can be differentiated term by term:

ddx(4x3−5x2+7)=12x2−10x.\frac{d}{dx}\big(4x^3 - 5x^2 + 7\big) = 12x^2 - 10x.dxd​(4x3−5x2+7)=12x2−10x.

Most functions are built with more than sums and constant multiples. x2sin⁡xx^2\sin xx2sinx is a product, 11+x2\dfrac{1}{1 + x^2}1+x21​ a quotient, and sin⁡(x2)\sin(x^2)sin(x2) and 1+x2\sqrt{1 + x^2}1+x2​ are compositions (Section 1.5). Each could be differentiated from the definition, with a new limit to work out every time. This module does that work once and for all: it proves one rule for each way of combining two functions, and it finds the derivatives of the trigonometric functions. After that, the derivative of a formula follows the way the formula is built.

2

The product rule

The derivative of a sum is the sum of the derivatives, so you might hope that the derivative of a product is the product of the derivatives. It is not. Take f(x)=xf(x) = xf(x)=x and g(x)=x2.g(x) = x^2\mathclose{\text{.}}g(x)=x2. Their product is x3,x^3\mathclose{\text{,}}x3, with derivative 3x2;3x^2\mathclose{\text{;}}3x2; the product of their derivatives is 1⋅2x=2x.1 \cdot 2x = 2x\mathclose{\text{.}}1⋅2x=2x. At x=1x = 1x=1 these are 3 and 2.

A growing rectangle

To find the right rule, picture a product as an area. Let u=f(x)u = f(x)u=f(x) and v=g(x)v = g(x)v=g(x) be the sides of a rectangle (for the picture, suppose they are positive), so that its area is A=uv.A = uv\mathclose{\text{.}}A=uv. When xxx increases by h,h\mathclose{\text{,}}h, the sides change by

Δu=f(x+h)−f(x),Δv=g(x+h)−g(x),\begin{aligned} \Delta u &= f(x + h) - f(x), \\ \Delta v &= g(x + h) - g(x), \end{aligned}ΔuΔv​=f(x+h)−f(x),=g(x+h)−g(x),​

and the area becomes (u+Δu)(v+Δv).(u + \Delta u)(v + \Delta v)\mathclose{\text{.}}(u+Δu)(v+Δv). Figure 5.1 cuts the new rectangle into the old one, a strip of area u Δvu\,\Delta vuΔv along the top, a strip of area v Δuv\,\Delta uvΔu down the side, and a small corner of area Δu Δv:\Delta u\,\Delta v\mathclose{\text{:}}ΔuΔv:

ΔA=(u+Δu)(v+Δv)−uv=u Δv+v Δu+Δu Δv.\begin{aligned} \Delta A &= (u + \Delta u)(v + \Delta v) - uv \\ &= u\,\Delta v + v\,\Delta u + \Delta u\,\Delta v. \end{aligned}ΔA​=(u+Δu)(v+Δv)−uv=uΔv+vΔu+ΔuΔv.​

Divide by hhh to get the average rate of change of the area:

ΔAh=u Δvh+v Δuh+Δu Δvh.\frac{\Delta A}{h} = u\,\frac{\Delta v}{h} + v\,\frac{\Delta u}{h} + \Delta u\,\frac{\Delta v}{h}.hΔA​=uhΔv​+vhΔu​+ΔuhΔv​.

As h→0,h \to 0\mathclose{\text{,}}h→0, Δv/h→g′(x)\Delta v/h \to g'(x)Δv/h→g′(x) and Δu/h→f′(x),\Delta u/h \to f'(x)\mathclose{\text{,}}Δu/h→f′(x), while Δu→0.\Delta u \to 0\mathclose{\text{.}}Δu→0. The corner is small in both directions, so even after division by hhh it disappears, and what is left is u g′(x)+v f′(x):u\,g'(x) + v\,f'(x)\mathclose{\text{:}}ug′(x)+vf′(x): each side’s rate of change times the other side.

Theorem 5.1The product rule

If fff and ggg are differentiable at x,x\mathclose{\text{,}}x, then so is their product fg,fg\mathclose{\text{,}}fg, and

(fg)′(x)=f′(x) g(x)+f(x) g′(x).(fg)'(x) = f'(x)\,g(x) + f(x)\,g'(x).(fg)′(x)=f′(x)g(x)+f(x)g′(x).

In Leibniz’s notation, with u=f(x)u = f(x)u=f(x) and v=g(x):v = g(x)\mathclose{\text{:}}v=g(x): ddx(uv)=dudx v+u dvdx.\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv) = \dfrac{du}{dx}\,v + u\,\dfrac{dv}{dx}\mathclose{\text{.}}dxd​(uv)=dxdu​v+udxdv​.

Proof

The proof turns the picture into limits. Write fff and ggg for f(x)f(x)f(x) and g(x),g(x)\mathclose{\text{,}}g(x), and for h≠0h \ne 0h=0 let Δf=f(x+h)−f(x)\Delta f = f(x + h) - f(x)Δf=f(x+h)−f(x) and Δg=g(x+h)−g(x),\Delta g = g(x + h) - g(x)\mathclose{\text{,}}Δg=g(x+h)−g(x), so that f(x+h)=f+Δff(x + h) = f + \Delta ff(x+h)=f+Δf and g(x+h)=g+Δg.g(x + h) = g + \Delta g\mathclose{\text{.}}g(x+h)=g+Δg. Expand the product, as in the rectangle, and divide by h:h\mathclose{\text{:}}h:

f(x+h) g(x+h)−fgh=(f+Δf)(g+Δg)−fgh=Δfh g+f Δgh+Δf Δgh.\begin{aligned} &\frac{f(x + h)\,g(x + h) - fg}{h} \\ &\quad= \frac{(f + \Delta f)(g + \Delta g) - fg}{h} \\ &\quad= \frac{\Delta f}{h}\,g + f\,\frac{\Delta g}{h} + \Delta f\,\frac{\Delta g}{h}. \end{aligned}​hf(x+h)g(x+h)−fg​=h(f+Δf)(g+Δg)−fg​=hΔf​g+fhΔg​+ΔfhΔg​.​

Now let h→0.h \to 0\mathclose{\text{.}}h→0. Since fff and ggg are differentiable at x,x\mathclose{\text{,}}x, Δf/h→f′(x)\Delta f/h \to f'(x)Δf/h→f′(x) and Δg/h→g′(x).\Delta g/h \to g'(x)\mathclose{\text{.}}Δg/h→g′(x). And Δf→0,\Delta f \to 0\mathclose{\text{,}}Δf→0, because a function that is differentiable at xxx is continuous there (Theorem 4.1). By the limit laws for sums and products, the expression approaches f′(x) g(x)+f(x) g′(x)+0⋅g′(x),f'(x)\,g(x) + f(x)\,g'(x) + 0\cdot g'(x)\mathclose{\text{,}}f′(x)g(x)+f(x)g′(x)+0⋅g′(x), which is the product rule.

∎

In words: the derivative of a product is the derivative of the first factor times the second, plus the first times the derivative of the second. The last term of the proof, Δf Δg/h,\Delta f\,\Delta g/h\mathclose{\text{,}}ΔfΔg/h, is the corner of the picture, and the continuity of fff is what makes it vanish.

The hypotheses are what the proof needs, not what a product needs in order to have a derivative. If fff or ggg is not differentiable at x,x\mathclose{\text{,}}x, the theorem says nothing: ∣x∣\abs{x}∣x∣ has no derivative at 0 (its graph has a corner there), but ∣x∣⋅∣x∣=x2\abs{x}\cdot\abs{x} = x^2∣x∣⋅∣x∣=x2 does.

Example 5.1Two ways to differentiate a product✓ Checked

Differentiate F(x)=(x2+1)(x3−2x)F(x) = (x^2 + 1)(x^3 - 2x)F(x)=(x2+1)(x3−2x) with the product rule, and check by expanding first.

With f(x)=x2+1f(x) = x^2 + 1f(x)=x2+1 and g(x)=x3−2x,g(x) = x^3 - 2x\mathclose{\text{,}}g(x)=x3−2x, the derivatives are f′(x)=2xf'(x) = 2xf′(x)=2x and g′(x)=3x2−2,g'(x) = 3x^2 - 2\mathclose{\text{,}}g′(x)=3x2−2, so

F′(x)=2x(x3−2x)+(x2+1)(3x2−2)=(2x4−4x2)+(3x4+x2−2)=5x4−3x2−2.\begin{aligned} F'(x) &= 2x(x^3 - 2x) \\ &\quad + (x^2 + 1)(3x^2 - 2) \\ &= (2x^4 - 4x^2) + (3x^4 + x^2 - 2) \\ &= 5x^4 - 3x^2 - 2. \end{aligned}F′(x)​=2x(x3−2x)+(x2+1)(3x2−2)=(2x4−4x2)+(3x4+x2−2)=5x4−3x2−2.​

Expanding first: F(x)=x5−2x3+x3−2x=x5−x3−2x,F(x) = x^5 - 2x^3 + x^3 - 2x = x^5 - x^3 - 2x\mathclose{\text{,}}F(x)=x5−2x3+x3−2x=x5−x3−2x, so F′(x)=5x4−3x2−2,F'(x) = 5x^4 - 3x^2 - 2\mathclose{\text{,}}F′(x)=5x4−3x2−2, the same.

Expanding works for polynomials. The product rule works for every product, including those that cannot be expanded, such as x2sin⁡xx^2\sin xx2sinx (Section 5.4), and it works with nothing but numbers.

Example 5.2Power in a circuit✓ Checked

The electrical power delivered to a component is P=VI,P = VI\mathclose{\text{,}}P=VI, the voltage across it times the current through it. Suppose that at some instant the voltage is 12 V and falling at 0.5 V per second, while the current is 2 A and rising at 0.1 A per second. Is the power rising or falling, and how fast?

VVV and III are functions of time t,t\mathclose{\text{,}}t, and at that instant V=12,V = 12\mathclose{\text{,}}V=12, V′=−0.5,V' = -0.5\mathclose{\text{,}}V′=−0.5, I=2I = 2I=2 and I′=0.1.I' = 0.1\mathclose{\text{.}}I′=0.1. By the product rule,

P′=V′I+VI′=(−0.5)(2)+(12)(0.1)=−1+1.2=0.2.\begin{aligned} P' &= V'I + VI' \\ &= (-0.5)(2) + (12)(0.1) \\ &= -1 + 1.2 = 0.2. \end{aligned}P′​=V′I+VI′=(−0.5)(2)+(12)(0.1)=−1+1.2=0.2.​

The power is rising, at 0.2 watts per second: the rising current outweighs the falling voltage.

Used twice, the product rule differentiates a product of three functions:

(fgk)′=((fg)k)′=(fg)′k+(fg)k′=f′gk+fg′k+fgk′.\begin{aligned} (fgk)' &= \big((fg)k\big)' = (fg)'k + (fg)k' \\ &= f'gk + fg'k + fgk'. \end{aligned}(fgk)′​=((fg)k)′=(fg)′k+(fg)k′=f′gk+fg′k+fgk′.​

Each term differentiates one factor and leaves the others alone; Exercise 5.10 takes this further.

Watch out

(fg)′=f′g′(fg)' = f'g'(fg)′=f′g′ is wrong, as x⋅x2x \cdot x^2x⋅x2 showed. Two ways to remember the right rule: each term differentiates exactly one factor; and in the rectangle, the change in each side sweeps out a strip along the other side.

The quotient rule

A quotient changes when its top changes and when its bottom changes, and the two effects pull in opposite directions: a larger numerator makes the fraction larger, a larger denominator makes it smaller. The rule has both, with a minus sign between them.

Theorem 5.2The quotient rule

If fff and ggg are differentiable at xxx and g(x)≠0,g(x) \ne 0\mathclose{\text{,}}g(x)=0, then f/gf/gf/g is differentiable at x,x\mathclose{\text{,}}x, and

(fg)′(x)=f′(x) g(x)−f(x) g′(x)g(x)2.\Big(\frac{f}{g}\Big)'(x) = \frac{f'(x)\,g(x) - f(x)\,g'(x)}{g(x)^2}.(gf​)′(x)=g(x)2f′(x)g(x)−f(x)g′(x)​.
Proof

First, f/gf/gf/g is defined near x:x\mathclose{\text{:}}x: ggg is continuous at x,x\mathclose{\text{,}}x, so for hhh close enough to 0, g(x+h)g(x + h)g(x+h) is close to g(x),g(x)\mathclose{\text{,}}g(x), which is not 0, and so g(x+h)≠0.g(x + h) \ne 0\mathclose{\text{.}}g(x+h)=0. For such h≠0,h \ne 0\mathclose{\text{,}}h=0, with f,f\mathclose{\text{,}}f, g,g\mathclose{\text{,}}g, Δf\Delta fΔf and Δg\Delta gΔg as in the proof of Theorem 5.1, put the two fractions over a common denominator:

f+Δfg+Δg−fg=(f+Δf) g−f (g+Δg)g (g+Δg)=Δf⋅g−f⋅Δgg (g+Δg).\begin{aligned} &\frac{f + \Delta f}{g + \Delta g} - \frac{f}{g} \\ &\quad= \frac{(f + \Delta f)\,g - f\,(g + \Delta g)}{g\,(g + \Delta g)} \\ &\quad= \frac{\Delta f\cdot g - f\cdot\Delta g}{g\,(g + \Delta g)}. \end{aligned}​g+Δgf+Δf​−gf​=g(g+Δg)(f+Δf)g−f(g+Δg)​=g(g+Δg)Δf⋅g−f⋅Δg​.​

Dividing by h,h\mathclose{\text{,}}h,

1h(f(x+h)g(x+h)−f(x)g(x))=Δfh g−f Δghg (g+Δg).\begin{aligned} &\frac{1}{h}\Big(\frac{f(x + h)}{g(x + h)} - \frac{f(x)}{g(x)}\Big) \\ &\quad= \frac{\dfrac{\Delta f}{h}\,g - f\,\dfrac{\Delta g}{h}}{g\,(g + \Delta g)}. \end{aligned}​h1​(g(x+h)f(x+h)​−g(x)f(x)​)=g(g+Δg)hΔf​g−fhΔg​​.​

As h→0,h \to 0\mathclose{\text{,}}h→0, Δf/h→f′(x)\Delta f/h \to f'(x)Δf/h→f′(x) and Δg/h→g′(x),\Delta g/h \to g'(x)\mathclose{\text{,}}Δg/h→g′(x), and Δg→0\Delta g \to 0Δg→0 because ggg is continuous at x.x\mathclose{\text{.}}x. So the denominator approaches g(x)2,g(x)^2\mathclose{\text{,}}g(x)2, which is not 0, and by the limit laws the expression approaches f′(x)g(x)−f(x)g′(x)g(x)2.\dfrac{f'(x)g(x) - f(x)g'(x)}{g(x)^2}\mathclose{\text{.}}g(x)2f′(x)g(x)−f(x)g′(x)​.

∎

The numerator is the product rule’s f′g+fg′f'g + fg'f′g+fg′ with a minus sign, so the order matters: the derivative of the top comes first. A rhyme helps some people: “low d-high minus high d-low, over the square of what’s below”.

Example 5.3A quotient of polynomials✓ Checked

Differentiate y=x2−1x2+1,y = \dfrac{x^2 - 1}{x^2 + 1}\mathclose{\text{,}}y=x2+1x2−1​, and find where its tangent line is horizontal.

The denominator x2+1x^2 + 1x2+1 is never 0, so the rule applies at every x.x\mathclose{\text{.}}x. Both x2−1x^2 - 1x2−1 and x2+1x^2 + 1x2+1 have derivative 2x:2x\mathclose{\text{:}}2x:

y′=2x(x2+1)−(x2−1)(2x)(x2+1)2=2x3+2x−2x3+2x(x2+1)2=4x(x2+1)2.\begin{aligned} y' &= \frac{2x(x^2 + 1) - (x^2 - 1)(2x)}{(x^2 + 1)^2} \\ &= \frac{2x^3 + 2x - 2x^3 + 2x}{(x^2 + 1)^2} \\ &= \frac{4x}{(x^2 + 1)^2}. \end{aligned}y′​=(x2+1)22x(x2+1)−(x2−1)(2x)​=(x2+1)22x3+2x−2x3+2x​=(x2+1)24x​.​

The tangent is horizontal where y′=0.y' = 0\mathclose{\text{.}}y′=0. A fraction is 0 when its numerator is 0, so 4x=0:4x = 0\mathclose{\text{:}}4x=0: only at x=0,x = 0\mathclose{\text{,}}x=0, the point (0,−1).(0, -1)\mathclose{\text{.}}(0,−1). It is the lowest point of the graph. Indeed, writing x2−1=(x2+1)−2x^2 - 1 = (x^2 + 1) - 2x2−1=(x2+1)−2 gives y=1−2x2+1;y = 1 - \dfrac{2}{x^2 + 1}\mathclose{\text{;}}y=1−x2+12​; since x2+1≥1,x^2 + 1 \ge 1\mathclose{\text{,}}x2+1≥1, the fraction is at most 2, so y≥1−2=−1.y \ge 1 - 2 = -1\mathclose{\text{.}}y≥1−2=−1. The slope is negative to the left of 0 and positive to the right.

Negative powers

The quotient rule completes the power rule for integers.

For every integer n,n\mathclose{\text{,}}n,

ddxxn=nxn−1,\frac{d}{dx}x^n = nx^{n-1},dxd​xn=nxn−1,

for every xxx if n≥1,n \ge 1\mathclose{\text{,}}n≥1, and for every x≠0x \ne 0x=0 if n≤0.n \le 0\mathclose{\text{.}}n≤0.

Proof

Module 4 proved the case n≥1.n \ge 1\mathclose{\text{.}}n≥1. For n=0,n = 0\mathclose{\text{,}}n=0, x0=1x^0 = 1x0=1 is constant, with derivative 0=0⋅x−1.0 = 0 \cdot x^{-1}\mathclose{\text{.}}0=0⋅x−1. ddx1xm=0⋅xm−1⋅mxm−1(xm)2=−mxm−1x2m=−mx−m−1,\begin{aligned} \frac{d}{dx}\frac{1}{x^m} &= \frac{0 \cdot x^m - 1 \cdot mx^{m-1}}{(x^m)^2} \\ &= \frac{-mx^{m-1}}{x^{2m}} = -mx^{-m-1}, \end{aligned}dxd​xm1​​=(xm)20⋅xm−1⋅mxm−1​=x2m−mxm−1​=−mx−m−1,​

and −mx−m−1=nxn−1.-mx^{-m-1} = nx^{n-1}\mathclose{\text{.}}−mx−m−1=nxn−1.

For example, ddx1x=ddxx−1=−x−2=−1x2,\dfrac{d}{dx}\dfrac{1}{x} = \dfrac{d}{dx}x^{-1} = -x^{-2} = -\dfrac{1}{x^2}\mathclose{\text{,}}dxd​x1​=dxd​x−1=−x−2=−x21​, the number that the difference quotients of 1/x1/x1/x approached in Exercise 1.9.

Example 5.4How fast gravity weakens✓ Checked

The gravitational pull between two bodies at distance rrr is F(r)=kr2,F(r) = \dfrac{k}{r^2}\mathclose{\text{,}}F(r)=r2k​, where k>0k > 0k>0 is a constant that depends on their masses. How fast does FFF change with r?r\mathclose{\text{?}}r?

Write F(r)=kr−2F(r) = kr^{-2}F(r)=kr−2 and use the power rule with n=−2:n = -2\mathclose{\text{:}}n=−2:

F′(r)=k⋅(−2)r−3=−2kr3.F'(r) = k \cdot (-2)r^{-3} = -\frac{2k}{r^3}.F′(r)=k⋅(−2)r−3=−r32k​.

The derivative is negative: the pull weakens as the distance grows. Compare it with FFF itself: F′(r)=−2r⋅kr2=−2rF(r).F'(r) = -\dfrac{2}{r}\cdot\dfrac{k}{r^2} = -\dfrac{2}{r}F(r)\mathclose{\text{.}}F′(r)=−r2​⋅r2k​=−r2​F(r). Near rrr the graph of FFF is close to its tangent line (Module 4), so a small step Δr\Delta rΔr outwards changes the pull by about

F′(r) Δr=−2 Δrr F(r):F'(r)\,\Delta r = -2\,\frac{\Delta r}{r}\,F(r):F′(r)Δr=−2rΔr​F(r):

moving 1% further away weakens the pull by about 2%. (Exactly: 1/1.012≈0.9803,1/1.01^2 \approx 0.9803\mathclose{\text{,}}1/1.012≈0.9803, a loss of about 1.97%.)

Watch out

(fg)′=f′g′\Big(\dfrac{f}{g}\Big)' = \dfrac{f'}{g'}(gf​)′=g′f′​ is wrong. For x≠0,x \ne 0\mathclose{\text{,}}x=0, x2x=x\dfrac{x^2}{x} = xxx2​=x has derivative 1, but (x2)′(x)′=2x1=2x.\dfrac{(x^2)'}{(x)'} = \dfrac{2x}{1} = 2x\mathclose{\text{.}}(x)′(x2)′​=12x​=2x. Keep the order in the numerator, f′g−fg′:f'g - fg'\mathclose{\text{:}}f′g−fg′: swapping it changes the sign of the answer. And use the simplest tool: for 3x4=3x−4\dfrac{3}{x^4} = 3x^{-4}x43​=3x−4 the power rule is quicker than the quotient rule, and for x3+x5,\dfrac{x^3 + x}{5}\mathclose{\text{,}}5x3+x​, with a constant denominator, the constant multiple rule is.

Derivatives of the trigonometric functions

Theorem 5.4Derivatives of sine and cosine

For every real number xxx (in radians),

ddxsin⁡x=cos⁡x,ddxcos⁡x=−sin⁡x.\begin{aligned} \frac{d}{dx}\sin x &= \cos x, \\ \frac{d}{dx}\cos x &= -\sin x. \end{aligned}dxd​sinxdxd​cosx​=cosx,=−sinx.​
Proof

By the addition formula sin⁡(x+h)=sin⁡xcos⁡h+cos⁡xsin⁡h\sin(x + h) = \sin x\cos h + \cos x\sin hsin(x+h)=sinxcosh+cosxsinh (Section 1.4),

sin⁡(x+h)−sin⁡xh=sin⁡xcos⁡h−sin⁡x+cos⁡xsin⁡hh=−sin⁡x⋅1−cos⁡hh+cos⁡x⋅sin⁡hh.\begin{aligned} &\frac{\sin(x + h) - \sin x}{h} \\ &\quad= \frac{\sin x\cos h - \sin x + \cos x\sin h}{h} \\ &\quad= -\sin x\cdot\frac{1 - \cos h}{h} + \cos x\cdot\frac{\sin h}{h}. \end{aligned}​hsin(x+h)−sinx​=hsinxcosh−sinx+cosxsinh​=−sinx⋅h1−cosh​+cosx⋅hsinh​.​

Here xxx is fixed and only hhh varies. As h→0h \to 0h→0 the two fractions approach 0 and 1 (Module 2), so the difference quotient approaches −sin⁡x⋅0+cos⁡x⋅1=cos⁡x.-\sin x \cdot 0 + \cos x \cdot 1 = \cos x\mathclose{\text{.}}−sinx⋅0+cosx⋅1=cosx.

For the cosine, the addition formula cos⁡(x+h)=cos⁡xcos⁡h−sin⁡xsin⁡h\cos(x + h) = \cos x\cos h - \sin x\sin hcos(x+h)=cosxcosh−sinxsinh gives in the same way

cos⁡(x+h)−cos⁡xh=−cos⁡x⋅1−cos⁡hh−sin⁡x⋅sin⁡hh,\begin{aligned} &\frac{\cos(x + h) - \cos x}{h} \\ &\quad= -\cos x\cdot\frac{1 - \cos h}{h} - \sin x\cdot\frac{\sin h}{h}, \end{aligned}​hcos(x+h)−cosx​=−cosx⋅h1−cosh​−sinx⋅hsinh​,​

which approaches −cos⁡x⋅0−sin⁡x⋅1=−sin⁡x.-\cos x \cdot 0 - \sin x \cdot 1 = -\sin x\mathclose{\text{.}}−cosx⋅0−sinx⋅1=−sinx.

∎

The minus sign in (cos⁡x)′=−sin⁡x(\cos x)' = -\sin x(cosx)′=−sinx shows in the graphs: for xxx a little above 0, the cosine falls from its crest, while sin⁡x\sin xsinx is positive.

Going deeperWhere the addition formulas come from

Module 1 quoted the addition formulas from school trigonometry. Here is a proof from the unit circle. Let PPP and QQQ be the points of the unit circle at angles xxx and y.y\mathclose{\text{.}}y. Turning the whole picture through the angle −y-y−y moves QQQ to (1,0)(1, 0)(1,0) and PPP to the point at angle x−y,x - y\mathclose{\text{,}}x−y, and turning does not change distances. So the squared distance from PPP to QQQ equals the squared distance from (cos⁡(x−y),sin⁡(x−y))\big(\cos(x - y), \sin(x - y)\big)(cos(x−y),sin(x−y)) to (1,0):(1, 0)\mathclose{\text{:}}(1,0):

(cos⁡x−cos⁡y)2+(sin⁡x−sin⁡y)2=(cos⁡(x−y)−1)2+sin⁡2(x−y).\begin{aligned} &(\cos x - \cos y)^2 + (\sin x - \sin y)^2 \\ &\quad= \big(\cos(x - y) - 1\big)^2 + \sin^2(x - y). \end{aligned}​(cosx−cosy)2+(sinx−siny)2=(cos(x−y)−1)2+sin2(x−y).​

Expand both sides and use sin⁡2θ+cos⁡2θ=1:\sin^2\theta + \cos^2\theta = 1\mathclose{\text{:}}sin2θ+cos2θ=1: the left side is 2−2(cos⁡xcos⁡y+sin⁡xsin⁡y)2 - 2(\cos x\cos y + \sin x\sin y)2−2(cosxcosy+sinxsiny) and the right side is 2−2cos⁡(x−y).2 - 2\cos(x - y)\mathclose{\text{.}}2−2cos(x−y). Hence

cos⁡(x−y)=cos⁡xcos⁡y+sin⁡xsin⁡y.\cos(x - y) = \cos x\cos y + \sin x\sin y.cos(x−y)=cosxcosy+sinxsiny.

Everything else follows from this. Replacing yyy by −y-y−y (cosine is even, sine is odd) gives the first formula below; taking x=π/2,x = \pi/2\mathclose{\text{,}}x=π/2, where the cosine is 0 and the sine is 1, gives the second:

cos⁡(x+y)=cos⁡xcos⁡y−sin⁡xsin⁡y,cos⁡(π2−y)=sin⁡y.\begin{aligned} \cos(x + y) &= \cos x\cos y - \sin x\sin y, \\ \cos(\tfrac{\pi}{2} - y) &= \sin y. \end{aligned}cos(x+y)cos(2π​−y)​=cosxcosy−sinxsiny,=siny.​

With π/2−y\pi/2 - yπ/2−y in place of y,y\mathclose{\text{,}}y, the second says sin⁡(π/2−y)=cos⁡y.\sin(\pi/2 - y) = \cos y\mathclose{\text{.}}sin(π/2−y)=cosy. Finally,

sin⁡(x+y)=cos⁡((π2−x)−y)=cos⁡(π2−x)cos⁡y+sin⁡(π2−x)sin⁡y=sin⁡xcos⁡y+cos⁡xsin⁡y.\begin{aligned} \sin(x + y) &= \cos\big((\tfrac{\pi}{2} - x) - y\big) \\ &= \cos(\tfrac{\pi}{2} - x)\cos y \\ &\quad + \sin(\tfrac{\pi}{2} - x)\sin y \\ &= \sin x\cos y + \cos x\sin y. \end{aligned}sin(x+y)​=cos((2π​−x)−y)=cos(2π​−x)cosy+sin(2π​−x)siny=sinxcosy+cosxsiny.​

Why radians. The limit sin⁡hh→1\dfrac{\sin h}{h} \to 1hsinh​→1 holds because hhh is measured in radians, as an arc of the unit circle (Module 2). In degrees, a stray factor π/180\pi/180π/180 appears in the derivative (Example 5.8). Radians are the unit in which the derivative of the sine is exactly the cosine.

The other four functions

The quotient rule gives the derivatives of the other four trigonometric functions from those of sine and cosine.

Theorem 5.5Derivatives of tan, cot, sec and csc

Where cos⁡x≠0,\cos x \ne 0\mathclose{\text{,}}cosx=0,

ddxtan⁡x=sec⁡2x,ddxsec⁡x=sec⁡xtan⁡x,\begin{aligned} \frac{d}{dx}\tan x &= \sec^2 x, \\ \frac{d}{dx}\sec x &= \sec x\tan x, \end{aligned}dxd​tanxdxd​secx​=sec2x,=secxtanx,​

and where sin⁡x≠0,\sin x \ne 0\mathclose{\text{,}}sinx=0,

ddxcot⁡x=−csc⁡2x,ddxcsc⁡x=−csc⁡xcot⁡x.\begin{aligned} \frac{d}{dx}\cot x &= -\csc^2 x, \\ \frac{d}{dx}\csc x &= -\csc x\cot x. \end{aligned}dxd​cotxdxd​cscx​=−csc2x,=−cscxcotx.​
Proof

Each is a quotient of the sine and the cosine (or of 1 and one of them), so use the quotient rule, then sin⁡2x+cos⁡2x=1.\sin^2 x + \cos^2 x = 1\mathclose{\text{.}}sin2x+cos2x=1. Where cos⁡x≠0,\cos x \ne 0\mathclose{\text{,}}cosx=0,

ddxsin⁡xcos⁡x=cos⁡xcos⁡x−sin⁡x(−sin⁡x)cos⁡2x=cos⁡2x+sin⁡2xcos⁡2x=1cos⁡2x=sec⁡2x,ddx1cos⁡x=0⋅cos⁡x−1⋅(−sin⁡x)cos⁡2x=1cos⁡x⋅sin⁡xcos⁡x=sec⁡xtan⁡x.\begin{aligned} &\frac{d}{dx}\frac{\sin x}{\cos x} \\ &\quad= \frac{\cos x\cos x - \sin x(-\sin x)}{\cos^2 x} \\ &\quad= \frac{\cos^2 x + \sin^2 x}{\cos^2 x} \\ &\quad= \frac{1}{\cos^2 x} = \sec^2 x, \\[6pt] &\frac{d}{dx}\frac{1}{\cos x} \\ &\quad= \frac{0\cdot\cos x - 1\cdot(-\sin x)}{\cos^2 x} \\ &\quad= \frac{1}{\cos x}\cdot\frac{\sin x}{\cos x} = \sec x\tan x. \end{aligned}​dxd​cosxsinx​=cos2xcosxcosx−sinx(−sinx)​=cos2xcos2x+sin2x​=cos2x1​=sec2x,dxd​cosx1​=cos2x0⋅cosx−1⋅(−sinx)​=cosx1​⋅cosxsinx​=secxtanx.​

Where sin⁡x≠0,\sin x \ne 0\mathclose{\text{,}}sinx=0,

ddxcos⁡xsin⁡x=(−sin⁡x)sin⁡x−cos⁡xcos⁡xsin⁡2x=−sin⁡2x+cos⁡2xsin⁡2x=−1sin⁡2x=−csc⁡2x,ddx1sin⁡x=0⋅sin⁡x−1⋅cos⁡xsin⁡2x=−1sin⁡x⋅cos⁡xsin⁡x=−csc⁡xcot⁡x.\begin{aligned} &\frac{d}{dx}\frac{\cos x}{\sin x} \\ &\quad= \frac{(-\sin x)\sin x - \cos x\cos x}{\sin^2 x} \\ &\quad= -\frac{\sin^2 x + \cos^2 x}{\sin^2 x} \\ &\quad= -\frac{1}{\sin^2 x} = -\csc^2 x, \\[6pt] &\frac{d}{dx}\frac{1}{\sin x} \\ &\quad= \frac{0\cdot\sin x - 1\cdot\cos x}{\sin^2 x} \\ &\quad= -\frac{1}{\sin x}\cdot\frac{\cos x}{\sin x} = -\csc x\cot x. \end{aligned}​dxd​sinxcosx​=sin2x(−sinx)sinx−cosxcosx​=−sin2xsin2x+cos2x​=−sin2x1​=−csc2x,dxd​sinx1​=sin2x0⋅sinx−1⋅cosx​=−sinx1​⋅sinxcosx​=−cscxcotx.​
∎

A pattern to remember: the three “co” functions, cosine, cotangent and cosecant, have the minus signs.

Differentiate (a) x2sin⁡x,x^2\sin x\mathclose{\text{,}}x2sinx, (b) sin⁡xcos⁡x,\sin x\cos x\mathclose{\text{,}}sinxcosx, and (c) sin⁡xx\dfrac{\sin x}{x}xsinx​ for x≠0.x \ne 0\mathclose{\text{.}}x=0.

Example 5.6A mass on a spring✓ Checked

A mass bounces on a spring. Suppose its height above its resting point after ttt seconds is s(t)=4sin⁡t+3cos⁡ts(t) = 4\sin t + 3\cos ts(t)=4sint+3cost centimetres. Find its velocity v=s′v = s'v=s′ and its acceleration a=v′,a = v'\mathclose{\text{,}}a=v′, and compare aaa with s.s\mathclose{\text{.}}s.

v(t)=4cos⁡t−3sin⁡t cm/s,a(t)=−4sin⁡t−3cos⁡t cm/s2.\begin{aligned} v(t) &= 4\cos t - 3\sin t \ \text{cm/s}, \\ a(t) &= -4\sin t - 3\cos t \ \text{cm/s}^2. \end{aligned}v(t)a(t)​=4cost−3sint cm/s,=−4sint−3cost cm/s2.​

So a(t)=−s(t)a(t) = -s(t)a(t)=−s(t) at every instant: the acceleration always points back towards the resting point, and is proportional to the distance from it. That is how a spring pulls (Hooke’s law), and Module 13 shows that every motion with this property is a combination of a sine and a cosine. At t=0t = 0t=0 the mass is 3 cm up and moving upwards at 4 cm/s.

Watch out

Two sign slips: (cos⁡x)′=−sin⁡x,(\cos x)' = -\sin x\mathclose{\text{,}}(cosx)′=−sinx, not sin⁡x;\sin x\mathclose{\text{;}}sinx; and the derivatives of cot⁡x\cot xcotx and csc⁡x\csc xcscx carry minus signs too. All six formulas assume radians: check them with a calculator in degree mode and they fail.

The chain rule

Compositions are everywhere: sin⁡(2x),\sin(2x)\mathclose{\text{,}}sin(2x), (x2+1)10,(x^2 + 1)^{10}\mathclose{\text{,}}(x2+1)10, 1+x2.\sqrt{1 + x^2}\mathclose{\text{.}}1+x2​. Start with numbers. What is the slope of y=sin⁡(2x)y = \sin(2x)y=sin(2x) at x=0?x = 0\mathclose{\text{?}}x=0? The difference quotients there are sin⁡(2h)−sin⁡0h=sin⁡(2h)h:\dfrac{\sin(2h) - \sin 0}{h} = \dfrac{\sin(2h)}{h}\mathclose{\text{:}}hsin(2h)−sin0​=hsin(2h)​:

hhhsin⁡(2h)h\dfrac{\sin(2h)}{h}hsin(2h)​
0.10.10.11.9866931.9866931.986693
0.010.010.011.9998671.9998671.999867
0.0010.0010.0011.9999991.9999991.999999

They approach 2, not cos⁡(2⋅0)=1.\cos(2 \cdot 0) = 1\mathclose{\text{.}}cos(2⋅0)=1. Section 1.5 explains why: the graph of sin⁡(2x)\sin(2x)sin(2x) is the graph of sin⁡x\sin xsinx squashed horizontally by the factor 2, so it climbs twice as steeply, and every slope doubles. The derivative of sin⁡(2x)\sin(2x)sin(2x) is 2cos⁡(2x):2\cos(2x)\mathclose{\text{:}}2cos(2x): the derivative of the outer function, the sine, evaluated at the inner function 2x,2x\mathclose{\text{,}}2x, times the rate 2 at which the inner function changes.

Rates multiply

In Figure 5.3, gear A has 36 teeth, gear B 18 and gear C 6. While A turns once, 36 teeth pass the point where it meets B, so B turns 36/18=236/18 = 236/18=2 times. For each turn of B, 18 teeth pass C, so C turns 18/6=318/6 = 318/6=3 times. So C turns 3⋅2=63 \cdot 2 = 63⋅2=6 times as fast as A. If θA,\theta_A\mathclose{\text{,}}θA​, θB\theta_BθB​ and θC\theta_CθC​ are the angles through which the gears have turned, each measured in its own direction of turning,

dθCdθA=dθCdθB⋅dθBdθA=3⋅2=6.\frac{d\theta_C}{d\theta_A} = \frac{d\theta_C}{d\theta_B}\cdot\frac{d\theta_B}{d\theta_A} = 3 \cdot 2 = 6.dθA​dθC​​=dθB​dθC​​⋅dθA​dθB​​=3⋅2=6.

Converting units works the same way. Suppose a car uses 0.06 litres of fuel per kilometre and drives at 90 km/h. Then it uses 0.06⋅90=5.40.06 \cdot 90 = 5.40.06⋅90=5.4 litres per hour, and the units cancel like fractions: (litres per km) times (km per hour) is litres per hour.

For gears and fuel the rates are constant. For curves they change from point to point, but near each point a differentiable function is close to its tangent line, which has a constant rate, its slope. So, point by point, the rates multiply.

Theorem 5.6The chain rule

If ggg is differentiable at xxx and fff is differentiable at g(x),g(x)\mathclose{\text{,}}g(x), then the composition F=f∘g,F = f \circ g\mathclose{\text{,}}F=f∘g, F(x)=f(g(x)),F(x) = f\big(g(x)\big)\mathclose{\text{,}}F(x)=f(g(x)), is differentiable at x,x\mathclose{\text{,}}x, and

F′(x)=f′(g(x)) g′(x).F'(x) = f'\big(g(x)\big)\,g'(x).F′(x)=f′(g(x))g′(x).

In Leibniz’s notation, with y=f(u)y = f(u)y=f(u) and u=g(x),u = g(x)\mathclose{\text{,}}u=g(x),

dydx=dydu⋅dudx,\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{dy}{du}\cdot\frac{du}{dx},dxdy​=dudy​⋅dxdu​,

where dy/dudy/dudy/du is evaluated at u=g(x).u = g(x)\mathclose{\text{.}}u=g(x).

In words: differentiate the outer function, leaving the inner function inside it unchanged, and multiply by the derivative of the inner function. The symbol f′(g(x))f'\big(g(x)\big)f′(g(x)) reads “f prime of g of x”: the derivative of f,f\mathclose{\text{,}}f, evaluated at the number g(x).g(x)\mathclose{\text{.}}g(x). The Leibniz form looks like cancelling du:du\mathclose{\text{:}}du: here dy/dxdy/dxdy/dx behaves like a fraction, which makes the rule easy to remember. It is not a proof, though, because dy/dudy/dudy/du is a single symbol for a limit (Module 4), not a fraction.

Note where fff must be differentiable: at g(x),g(x)\mathclose{\text{,}}g(x), the point where it is used, not at x.x\mathclose{\text{.}}x. Without that hypothesis the rule can fail: with f(u)=∣u∣f(u) = \abs{u}f(u)=∣u∣ and g(x)=x2−1,g(x) = x^2 - 1\mathclose{\text{,}}g(x)=x2−1, fff is differentiable at 1 but not at g(1)=0,g(1) = 0\mathclose{\text{,}}g(1)=0, and f(g(x))=∣x2−1∣f\big(g(x)\big) = \abs{x^2 - 1}f(g(x))=​x2−1​ has a corner at x=1.x = 1\mathclose{\text{.}}x=1.

The idea of the proof. Let u=g(x),u = g(x)\mathclose{\text{,}}u=g(x), and when xxx changes by h,h\mathclose{\text{,}}h, let Δu=g(x+h)−g(x)\Delta u = g(x + h) - g(x)Δu=g(x+h)−g(x) and Δy=f(u+Δu)−f(u)\Delta y = f(u + \Delta u) - f(u)Δy=f(u+Δu)−f(u) be the changes in uuu and in y.y\mathclose{\text{.}}y. If Δu≠0,\Delta u \ne 0\mathclose{\text{,}}Δu=0,

Δyh=ΔyΔu⋅Δuh.\frac{\Delta y}{h} = \frac{\Delta y}{\Delta u}\cdot\frac{\Delta u}{h}.hΔy​=ΔuΔy​⋅hΔu​.

As h→0,h \to 0\mathclose{\text{,}}h→0, Δu→0\Delta u \to 0Δu→0 (because ggg is continuous at x),x\mathclose{\text{),}}x), so Δy/Δu→f′(u),\Delta y/\Delta u \to f'(u)\mathclose{\text{,}}Δy/Δu→f′(u), while Δu/h→g′(x);\Delta u/h \to g'(x)\mathclose{\text{;}}Δu/h→g′(x); the product approaches f′(u) g′(x).f'(u)\,g'(x)\mathclose{\text{.}}f′(u)g′(x). This is the gear argument with limits, and it is almost a proof. The gap: Δu\Delta uΔu can be 0 for values of h≠0h \ne 0h=0 as close to 0 as you like (for a constant g,g\mathclose{\text{,}}g, it is 0 for every h;h\mathclose{\text{;}}h; Exercise 5.11 gives a less obvious example), and then Δy/Δu\Delta y/\Delta uΔy/Δu is 0/0.0/0\mathclose{\text{.}}0/0. The next box closes the gap with a complete proof; a first reading may skip it.

Going deeperA proof of the chain rule

The way round the division by Δu\Delta uΔu is to describe the differentiability of fff without dividing. Let u=g(x).u = g(x)\mathclose{\text{.}}u=g(x). Since fff is differentiable at u,u\mathclose{\text{,}}u, it is defined on an open interval around u;u\mathclose{\text{;}}u; for k≠0k \ne 0k=0 with u+ku + ku+k in that interval, let

E(k)=f(u+k)−f(u)k−f′(u),E(k) = \frac{f(u + k) - f(u)}{k} - f'(u),E(k)=kf(u+k)−f(u)​−f′(u),

the amount by which the difference quotient exceeds f′(u),f'(u)\mathclose{\text{,}}f′(u), and let E(0)=0.E(0) = 0\mathclose{\text{.}}E(0)=0. That fff is differentiable at uuu says exactly that E(k)→0E(k) \to 0E(k)→0 as k→0;k \to 0\mathclose{\text{;}}k→0; since E(0)=0,E(0) = 0\mathclose{\text{,}}E(0)=0, EEE is continuous at 0. Multiplying by k,k\mathclose{\text{,}}k,

f(u+k)−f(u)=(f′(u)+E(k)) k,f(u + k) - f(u) = \big(f'(u) + E(k)\big)\,k,f(u+k)−f(u)=(f′(u)+E(k))k,

for k≠0,k \ne 0\mathclose{\text{,}}k=0, and also for k=0,k = 0\mathclose{\text{,}}k=0, when both sides are 0.

Now let h≠0h \ne 0h=0 be small enough that g(x+h)g(x + h)g(x+h) lies in the interval (possible because ggg is continuous at x),x\mathclose{\text{),}}x), and put k=Δu=g(x+h)−g(x),k = \Delta u = g(x + h) - g(x)\mathclose{\text{,}}k=Δu=g(x+h)−g(x), which is allowed whether Δu\Delta uΔu is 0 or not. Dividing by h,h\mathclose{\text{,}}h,

f(g(x+h))−f(g(x))h=(f′(u)+E(Δu)) Δuh.\begin{aligned} &\frac{f\big(g(x + h)\big) - f\big(g(x)\big)}{h} \\ &\quad= \big(f'(u) + E(\Delta u)\big)\,\frac{\Delta u}{h}. \end{aligned}​hf(g(x+h))−f(g(x))​=(f′(u)+E(Δu))hΔu​.​

Let h→0.h \to 0\mathclose{\text{.}}h→0. Then Δu/h→g′(x),\Delta u/h \to g'(x)\mathclose{\text{,}}Δu/h→g′(x), since ggg is differentiable at x.x\mathclose{\text{.}}x. Also Δu→0,\Delta u \to 0\mathclose{\text{,}}Δu→0, since ggg is continuous at x,x\mathclose{\text{,}}x, and therefore E(Δu)→E(0)=0,E(\Delta u) \to E(0) = 0\mathclose{\text{,}}E(Δu)→E(0)=0, since EEE is continuous at 0 (the limit of a composition, Theorem 3.4). So the right side approaches f′(u) g′(x),f'(u)\,g'(x)\mathclose{\text{,}}f′(u)g′(x), which proves the chain rule.

Each hypothesis was used: the differentiability of ggg at x,x\mathclose{\text{,}}x, for Δu/h→g′(x)\Delta u/h \to g'(x)Δu/h→g′(x) and, through continuity, for Δu→0;\Delta u \to 0\mathclose{\text{;}}Δu→0; and the differentiability of fff at u=g(x),u = g(x)\mathclose{\text{,}}u=g(x), not at x,x\mathclose{\text{,}}x, for E(k)→0.E(k) \to 0\mathclose{\text{.}}E(k)→0.

Using the chain rule

To use the chain rule, name the inner function, differentiate the outer function with the inner one left inside, and multiply by the inner derivative.

Example 5.7Three compositions✓ Checked

Differentiate (a) (2x+1)5,(2x + 1)^5\mathclose{\text{,}}(2x+1)5, (b) sin⁡(x2)\sin(x^2)sin(x2) and (c) sin⁡2x.\sin^2 x\mathclose{\text{.}}sin2x.

(a) The inner function is u=2x+1,u = 2x + 1\mathclose{\text{,}}u=2x+1, with du/dx=2,du/dx = 2\mathclose{\text{,}}du/dx=2, and the outer function is u5:u^5\mathclose{\text{:}}u5:

ddx(2x+1)5=5(2x+1)4⋅2=10(2x+1)4.\begin{aligned} \frac{d}{dx}(2x + 1)^5 &= 5(2x + 1)^4 \cdot 2 \\ &= 10(2x + 1)^4. \end{aligned}dxd​(2x+1)5​=5(2x+1)4⋅2=10(2x+1)4.​

Expanding (2x+1)5(2x + 1)^5(2x+1)5 first would also work, with much more effort.

(b) Inner u=x2,u = x^2\mathclose{\text{,}}u=x2, outer sin⁡u:\sin u\mathclose{\text{:}}sinu: ddxsin⁡(x2)=cos⁡(x2)⋅2x=2xcos⁡(x2).\dfrac{d}{dx}\sin(x^2) = \cos(x^2)\cdot 2x = 2x\cos(x^2)\mathclose{\text{.}}dxd​sin(x2)=cos(x2)⋅2x=2xcos(x2).

(c) sin⁡2x\sin^2 xsin2x means (sin⁡x)2:(\sin x)^2\mathclose{\text{:}}(sinx)2: inner u=sin⁡x,u = \sin x\mathclose{\text{,}}u=sinx, outer u2.u^2\mathclose{\text{.}}u2. So ddxsin⁡2x=2sin⁡x⋅cos⁡x.\dfrac{d}{dx}\sin^2 x = 2\sin x\cdot\cos x\mathclose{\text{.}}dxd​sin2x=2sinx⋅cosx.

In (b) the sine is outside and in (c) inside: the same two functions, composed in the two orders, have different derivatives.

Example 5.8Sine in degrees✓ Checked

In degree mode, a calculator’s sine key computes S(x)=sin⁡(x∘)=sin⁡(πx180).S(x) = \sin(x^\circ) = \sin\Big(\dfrac{\pi x}{180}\Big)\mathclose{\text{.}}S(x)=sin(x∘)=sin(180πx​). Find S′(x).S'(x)\mathclose{\text{.}}S′(x).

S′(x)=cos⁡(πx180)⋅π180=π180cos⁡(x∘).\begin{aligned} S'(x) &= \cos\Big(\frac{\pi x}{180}\Big)\cdot\frac{\pi}{180} \\ &= \frac{\pi}{180}\cos(x^\circ). \end{aligned}S′(x)​=cos(180πx​)⋅180π​=180π​cos(x∘).​

At x=0x = 0x=0 the slope is π/180≈0.017453\pi/180 \approx 0.017453π/180≈0.017453 per degree. Every derivative of a trigonometric function would carry this factor if angles were measured in degrees.

The chain rule extends to longer chains: apply it once for each link, working from the outside in.

Example 5.9A chain of three links✓ Checked

Differentiate y=sin⁡3(4x),y = \sin^3(4x)\mathclose{\text{,}}y=sin3(4x), which means (sin⁡(4x))3.\big(\sin(4x)\big)^3\mathclose{\text{.}}(sin(4x))3.

dydx=dydu⋅dudv⋅dvdx=3u2⋅cos⁡v⋅4=12sin⁡2(4x)cos⁡(4x).\begin{aligned} \frac{dy}{dx} &= \frac{dy}{du}\cdot\frac{du}{dv}\cdot\frac{dv}{dx} = 3u^2\cdot\cos v\cdot 4 \\ &= 12\sin^2(4x)\cos(4x). \end{aligned}dxdy​​=dudy​⋅dvdu​⋅dxdv​=3u2⋅cosv⋅4=12sin2(4x)cos(4x).​

In one line: the cube first, bringing down a 3 and leaving sin⁡(4x)\sin(4x)sin(4x) inside; then the sine, leaving 4x4x4x inside; then 4x4x4x itself.

6

Combining the rules

Real formulas combine several rules. A systematic order keeps the work under control.

Key idea

To differentiate a formula:

  1. Rewrite it if that helps. Use negative powers for reciprocals (3x4=3x−4);\dfrac{3}{x^4} = 3x^{-4}\mathclose{\text{);}}x43​=3x−4); cancel common factors, noting the points left out; expand a short product of polynomials.
  2. Find the last operation: the one you would carry out last when computing the formula’s value at a number. It chooses the rule: a sum, the sum rule; a product, the product rule; a quotient, the quotient rule; a function applied to something other than xxx itself, the chain rule.
  3. Apply that rule, and treat each piece it leaves to differentiate in the same way, until only the basic derivatives remain.
  4. Simplify: take out common factors, combine fractions, use identities such as sin⁡2x+cos⁡2x=1,\sin^2 x + \cos^2 x = 1\mathclose{\text{,}}sin2x+cos2x=1, and say where the result holds.
  5. Check it: at a point with a difference quotient, on a graph (the grapher below), or with SymPy (Section 5.7).
Formula Last operation First rule
x2sin⁡xx^2\sin xx2sinx multiply x2x^2x2 by sin⁡x\sin xsinx product
sin⁡(x2)\sin(x^2)sin(x2) take the sine of x2x^2x2 chain
sin⁡2x\sin^2 xsin2x square sin⁡x\sin xsinx chain
xsin⁡x\dfrac{x}{\sin x}sinxx​ divide xxx by sin⁡x\sin xsinx quotient
sin⁡xcos⁡(3x)\sin x\cos(3x)sinxcos(3x) multiply product, then chain for cos⁡(3x)\cos(3x)cos(3x)
Example 5.12A product of powers✓ Checked

Differentiate y=x3(2x−1)4,y = x^3(2x - 1)^4\mathclose{\text{,}}y=x3(2x−1)4, simplify, and find where the tangent is horizontal.

The last operation is the product of x3x^3x3 and (2x−1)4.(2x - 1)^4\mathclose{\text{.}}(2x−1)4. The second factor needs the chain rule: its derivative is 4(2x−1)3⋅2=8(2x−1)3.4(2x - 1)^3 \cdot 2 = 8(2x - 1)^3\mathclose{\text{.}}4(2x−1)3⋅2=8(2x−1)3. So

y′=3x2(2x−1)4+x3⋅8(2x−1)3.y' = 3x^2(2x - 1)^4 + x^3 \cdot 8(2x - 1)^3.y′=3x2(2x−1)4+x3⋅8(2x−1)3.

Both terms contain x2(2x−1)3;x^2(2x - 1)^3\mathclose{\text{;}}x2(2x−1)3; take it out:

y′=x2(2x−1)3[3(2x−1)+8x]=x2(2x−1)3(14x−3).\begin{aligned} y' &= x^2(2x - 1)^3\big[3(2x - 1) + 8x\big] \\ &= x^2(2x - 1)^3(14x - 3). \end{aligned}y′​=x2(2x−1)3[3(2x−1)+8x]=x2(2x−1)3(14x−3).​

The factored form shows at once where y′=0:y' = 0\mathclose{\text{:}}y′=0: at x=0,x = 0\mathclose{\text{,}}x=0, x=12x = \tfrac12x=21​ and x=314.x = \tfrac{3}{14}\mathclose{\text{.}}x=143​. The tangent is horizontal at these three points. The expanded form, 112x6−192x5+120x4−32x3+3x2,112x^6 - 192x^5 + 120x^4 - 32x^3 + 3x^2\mathclose{\text{,}}112x6−192x5+120x4−32x3+3x2, hides this.

Example 5.13A quotient that simplifies✓ Checked

Differentiate y=sin⁡x1+cos⁡x,y = \dfrac{\sin x}{1 + \cos x}\mathclose{\text{,}}y=1+cosxsinx​, where cos⁡x≠−1.\cos x \ne -1\mathclose{\text{.}}cosx=−1.

The quotient rule, then the Pythagorean identity in the numerator:

y′=cos⁡x (1+cos⁡x)−sin⁡x (−sin⁡x)(1+cos⁡x)2=cos⁡x+cos⁡2x+sin⁡2x(1+cos⁡x)2=1+cos⁡x(1+cos⁡x)2=11+cos⁡x.\begin{aligned} y' &= \frac{\cos x\,(1 + \cos x) - \sin x\,(-\sin x)}{(1 + \cos x)^2} \\ &= \frac{\cos x + \cos^2 x + \sin^2 x}{(1 + \cos x)^2} \\ &= \frac{1 + \cos x}{(1 + \cos x)^2} = \frac{1}{1 + \cos x}. \end{aligned}y′​=(1+cosx)2cosx(1+cosx)−sinx(−sinx)​=(1+cosx)2cosx+cos2x+sin2x​=(1+cosx)21+cosx​=1+cosx1​.​
Example 5.14A chain around a quotient✓ Checked

Differentiate y=(x−1x+1)4,y = \Big(\dfrac{x - 1}{x + 1}\Big)^4\mathclose{\text{,}}y=(x+1x−1​)4, for x≠−1.x \ne -1\mathclose{\text{.}}x=−1.

The last operation is the fourth power, so the chain rule comes first, with the quotient as the inner function. Its derivative, by the quotient rule, is

ddxx−1x+1=1⋅(x+1)−(x−1)⋅1(x+1)2=2(x+1)2,\begin{aligned} \frac{d}{dx}\frac{x - 1}{x + 1} &= \frac{1\cdot(x + 1) - (x - 1)\cdot 1}{(x + 1)^2} \\ &= \frac{2}{(x + 1)^2}, \end{aligned}dxd​x+1x−1​​=(x+1)21⋅(x+1)−(x−1)⋅1​=(x+1)22​,​

so

y′=4(x−1x+1)3⋅2(x+1)2=8(x−1)3(x+1)5.\begin{aligned} y' &= 4\Big(\frac{x - 1}{x + 1}\Big)^3\cdot\frac{2}{(x + 1)^2} \\ &= \frac{8(x - 1)^3}{(x + 1)^5}. \end{aligned}y′​=4(x+1x−1​)3⋅(x+1)22​=(x+1)58(x−1)3​.​

Watch out

Simplify a function before you differentiate it when that is cheap, but keep track of what the simplification assumes. For x≠1,x \ne 1\mathclose{\text{,}}x=1, x2−1x−1=x+1,\dfrac{x^2 - 1}{x - 1} = x + 1\mathclose{\text{,}}x−1x2−1​=x+1, so its derivative is 1 at every x≠1;x \ne 1\mathclose{\text{;}}x=1; at x=1x = 1x=1 the function is not defined, so it has no derivative there. And an unsimplified answer is not wrong, only harder to use: Example 5.12 needed the factored form to find where the tangent is horizontal.

7

Derivatives with SymPy

SymPy’s diff (Module 4) knows every rule of this module. sp.diff(expr, x) differentiates expr with respect to x; sp.factor and sp.simplify (Module 1) tidy the result.

Compute itDifferentiating with SymPy
Python
import sympy as sp
x = sp.symbols('x')
y = x**3*(2*x - 1)**4            # Example 5.12
dy = sp.diff(y, x)
print(dy)
print(sp.factor(dy))
print(sp.expand(dy))
Output
8*x**3*(2*x - 1)**3 + 3*x**2*(2*x - 1)**4
x**2*(2*x - 1)**3*(14*x - 3)
112*x**6 - 192*x**5 + 120*x**4 - 32*x**3 + 3*x**2

The first line is the product rule’s answer before any simplifying, with the terms in SymPy’s order; factor gives the form of Example 5.12, and expand the expanded form, correct but no help in finding where y′=0.y' = 0\mathclose{\text{.}}y′=0. SymPy also applies the rules to functions it knows nothing about:

Python
f, g = sp.Function('f'), sp.Function('g')
print(sp.diff(f(x)*g(x), x))
print(sp.diff(f(g(x)), x))
print(sp.diff(sp.tan(x), x))
Output
f(x)*Derivative(g(x), x) + g(x)*Derivative(f(x), x)
Derivative(f(g(x)), g(x))*Derivative(g(x), x)
tan(x)**2 + 1

The first line is the product rule and the second the chain rule: Derivative(f(g(x)), g(x)) means f′f'f′ evaluated at g(x).g(x)\mathclose{\text{.}}g(x). The third is sec⁡2x\sec^2 xsec2x in disguise: dividing sin⁡2x+cos⁡2x=1\sin^2 x + \cos^2 x = 1sin2x+cos2x=1 by cos⁡2x\cos^2 xcos2x gives tan⁡2x+1=sec⁡2x.\tan^2 x + 1 = \sec^2 x\mathclose{\text{.}}tan2x+1=sec2x.

SymPy differentiates SymPy expressions only. Python’s math.sin works with numbers, so it fails on a symbol:

Pythonraises an error on purpose
import math
print(sp.diff(math.sin(x), x))
Error
TypeError: Cannot convert expression to float

Use sp.sin, sp.cos, sp.sqrt and the other SymPy functions in formulas you want to differentiate.

Why the answers can look different

SymPy applies the rules mechanically and tidies up only a little. Its answer and yours can differ in the order of the terms, in how they are grouped, in which identities were used (tan⁡2x+1\tan^2 x + 1tan2x+1 for sec⁡2x,\sec^2 x\mathclose{\text{,}}sec2x, or cos⁡2x−sin⁡2x\cos^2 x - \sin^2 xcos2x−sin2x for cos⁡2x,\cos 2x\mathclose{\text{,}}cos2x, the addition formula with y=x),y = x\mathclose{\text{),}}y=x), or because one of you simplified and the other did not. Two expressions AAA and BBB are equal exactly when A−B=0,A - B = 0\mathclose{\text{,}}A−B=0, so to compare two answers, simplify their difference.

Compute itIs my answer right?
Python
import sympy as sp
x = sp.symbols('x')
theirs = sp.diff(sp.sin(x)/(1 + sp.cos(x)), x)     # Example 5.13
mine = 1/(1 + sp.cos(x))
print(theirs)
print(sp.simplify(theirs - mine))
Output
cos(x)/(cos(x) + 1) + sin(x)**2/(cos(x) + 1)**2
0

The difference simplifies to 0, so the answers agree. A wrong answer leaves something behind. Suppose you forgot the inner derivative of sin⁡(x2)\sin(x^2)sin(x2) and wrote cos⁡(x2):\cos(x^2)\mathclose{\text{:}}cos(x2):

Python
wrong = sp.cos(x**2)
gap = sp.simplify(sp.diff(sp.sin(x**2), x) - wrong)
print(gap)
print([round(float(gap.subs(x, v)), 4) for v in (0.5, 1, 2)])
Output
(2*x - 1)*cos(x**2)
[0.0, 0.5403, -1.9609]

The last line evaluates the difference at three numbers. At x=0.5x = 0.5x=0.5 the wrong answer happens to be right, because 2x−1=02x - 1 = 02x−1=0 there; at 1 and 2 it is not, and one non-zero value is enough to prove two expressions different.

Key idea

To check that two answers AAA and BBB are equal, simplify A−B.A - B\mathclose{\text{.}}A−B. If you get 0, they are equal wherever both are defined. If not, evaluate A−BA - BA−B at a few numbers: a value that is not 0 proves them different. simplify does not find every simplification, so a difference that does not simplify to 0 does not by itself prove the answers different; a non-zero value does.

Watch out

A difference that is 0 at one or two points proves nothing: (2x−1)cos⁡(x2)(2x - 1)\cos(x^2)(2x−1)cos(x2) is 0 at x=0.5.x = 0.5\mathclose{\text{.}}x=0.5. Test several points, not round numbers only, or simplify.

8

Automatic differentiation

Training a neural network, fitting a model to data, steering a robot arm: each needs derivatives of functions that exist only as programs, often long ones with loops and branches. How can one program differentiate another? There are three ways.

  • Finite differences (Module 4): run the program at aaa and at a+h,a + h\mathclose{\text{,}}a+h, and compute f(a+h)−f(a)h.\dfrac{f(a + h) - f(a)}{h}\mathclose{\text{.}}hf(a+h)−f(a)​. This needs nothing but the program, but it is an approximation: a large hhh gives a truncation error, a small one a rounding error, and the best compromise keeps only about half of the 16 significant digits that floating-point numbers carry.
  • Symbolic differentiation, as in SymPy: turn the program into a formula and apply the rules of this module. The result is exact, but the formulas can grow very large, and loops and branches must first be turned into a formula.
  • Automatic differentiation: run the program once, on numbers that carry a derivative along with their value, updated at every step by the rules of this module. There is no step hhh and so no truncation error: the result is exact apart from floating-point rounding, of the kind that affects the value of fff itself, and it costs a few extra operations per step.

The simplest way to carry derivatives along is with dual numbers.

Definition 5.1Dual numbers

A dual number is an expression a+bε,a + b\varepsilon\mathclose{\text{,}}a+bε, where aaa and bbb are real numbers and ε\varepsilonε (the Greek letter epsilon) is a new symbol with ε2=0.\varepsilon^2 = 0\mathclose{\text{.}}ε2=0. Dual numbers are added and multiplied like polynomials in ε,\varepsilon\mathclose{\text{,}}ε, with ε2\varepsilon^2ε2 replaced by 0:

(a+bε)+(c+dε)=(a+c)+(b+d)ε,(a+bε)(c+dε)=ac+(ad+bc)ε.\begin{aligned} &(a + b\varepsilon) + (c + d\varepsilon) \\ &\quad= (a + c) + (b + d)\varepsilon, \\ &(a + b\varepsilon)(c + d\varepsilon) \\ &\quad= ac + (ad + bc)\varepsilon. \end{aligned}​(a+bε)+(c+dε)=(a+c)+(b+d)ε,(a+bε)(c+dε)=ac+(ad+bc)ε.​

A real number ccc is the dual number c+0ε;c + 0\varepsilon\mathclose{\text{;}}c+0ε; bbb is the ε\varepsilonε-part of a+bε.a + b\varepsilon\mathclose{\text{.}}a+bε.

No real number except 0 has square 0, so ε\varepsilonε is not a real number: it is a symbol with one rule. (Books on automatic differentiation use the letter ε\varepsilonε for it; it has nothing to do with the ε\varepsilonε of Module 2’s limits or the machine epsilon of Module 4.) Look at the product. Its ε\varepsilonε-part, ad+bc,ad + bc\mathclose{\text{,}}ad+bc, is the product rule: if aaa and ccc are the values of two functions and bbb and ddd their derivatives, then the product has value acacac and derivative ad+bc.ad + bc\mathclose{\text{.}}ad+bc. That is the whole trick.

Theorem 5.7Dual numbers carry derivatives

If ppp is a polynomial, then for all real numbers aaa and b,b\mathclose{\text{,}}b,

p(a+bε)=p(a)+p′(a) b ε.p(a + b\varepsilon) = p(a) + p'(a)\,b\,\varepsilon.p(a+bε)=p(a)+p′(a)bε.

In particular, the ε\varepsilonε-part of p(a+ε)p(a + \varepsilon)p(a+ε) is the derivative p′(a).p'(a)\mathclose{\text{.}}p′(a).

Proof

A polynomial is built from constants and xxx by additions and multiplications. Call a function qqq good if q(a+bε)=q(a)+q′(a) b εq(a + b\varepsilon) = q(a) + q'(a)\,b\,\varepsilonq(a+bε)=q(a)+q′(a)bε for all aaa and b.b\mathclose{\text{.}}b. A constant ccc is good, since c=c+0εc = c + 0\varepsilonc=c+0ε and c′=0;c' = 0\mathclose{\text{;}}c′=0; so is x,x\mathclose{\text{,}}x, since x′=1.x' = 1\mathclose{\text{.}}x′=1. If qqq and rrr are good, then q+rq + rq+r is good, by the sum rule, and so is qr:qr\mathclose{\text{:}}qr:

q(a+bε) r(a+bε)=(q(a)+q′(a)bε)⋅(r(a)+r′(a)bε)=q(a)r(a)+(q′(a)r(a)+q(a)r′(a))bε,\begin{aligned} &q(a + b\varepsilon)\,r(a + b\varepsilon) \\ &\quad= \big(q(a) + q'(a)b\varepsilon\big) \\ &\qquad \cdot \big(r(a) + r'(a)b\varepsilon\big) \\ &\quad= q(a)r(a) \\ &\qquad + \big(q'(a)r(a) + q(a)r'(a)\big)b\varepsilon, \end{aligned}​q(a+bε)r(a+bε)=(q(a)+q′(a)bε)⋅(r(a)+r′(a)bε)=q(a)r(a)+(q′(a)r(a)+q(a)r′(a))bε,​

which is (qr)(a)+(qr)′(a) b ε(qr)(a) + (qr)'(a)\,b\,\varepsilon(qr)(a)+(qr)′(a)bε by the product rule. Every step of building ppp keeps it good, so ppp is good.

∎

For example, (3+ε)2=9+6ε+ε2=9+6ε,(3 + \varepsilon)^2 = 9 + 6\varepsilon + \varepsilon^2 = 9 + 6\varepsilon\mathclose{\text{,}}(3+ε)2=9+6ε+ε2=9+6ε, and x2x^2x2 has value 9 and derivative 6 at x=3.x = 3\mathclose{\text{.}}x=3.

Other functions join in by declaring their own derivative. For the sine, define sin⁡(a+bε)=sin⁡a+(cos⁡a) b ε.\sin(a + b\varepsilon) = \sin a + (\cos a)\,b\,\varepsilon\mathclose{\text{.}}sin(a+bε)=sina+(cosa)bε. Then for a good function g,g\mathclose{\text{,}}g,

sin⁡(g(a+bε))=sin⁡(g(a)+g′(a) b ε)=sin⁡g(a)+cos⁡g(a) g′(a) b ε,\begin{aligned} &\sin\big(g(a + b\varepsilon)\big) \\ &\quad= \sin\big(g(a) + g'(a)\,b\,\varepsilon\big) \\ &\quad= \sin g(a) + \cos g(a)\,g'(a)\,b\,\varepsilon, \end{aligned}​sin(g(a+bε))=sin(g(a)+g′(a)bε)=sing(a)+cosg(a)g′(a)bε,​

whose ε\varepsilonε-part is the chain rule’s (sin⁡g)′(a)(\sin g)'(a)(sing)′(a) times b.b\mathclose{\text{.}}b. Each operation in the program knows only its own derivative; the chain rule, applied step by step as the program runs, does the rest.

Compute itDual numbers in Python

A class with two numbers, the value a and the ε\varepsilonε-part b, and the rules of Definition 5.1 for + and *:

Python
class Dual:
    """A dual number a + b·ε, where ε² = 0."""
    def __init__(self, a, b=0.0):
        self.a, self.b = a, b              # the value and the ε-part
    def __add__(self, other):
        other = other if isinstance(other, Dual) else Dual(other)
        return Dual(self.a + other.a, self.b + other.b)
    def __mul__(self, other):
        other = other if isinstance(other, Dual) else Dual(other)
        return Dual(self.a*other.a, self.a*other.b + self.b*other.a)
    __radd__ = __add__                     # 1 + d and 3*d: number first
    __rmul__ = __mul__

Python calls __add__ for + and __mul__ for *, so any function written with + and * now works on dual numbers. Take f(x)=x3−2x+1f(x) = x^3 - 2x + 1f(x)=x3−2x+1 at x=1.5,x = 1.5\mathclose{\text{,}}x=1.5, and run it on 1.5+1ε:1.5 + 1\varepsilon\mathclose{\text{:}}1.5+1ε:

Python
def f(x):
    return x*x*x + (-2)*x + 1          # x³ − 2x + 1, with + and * only

y = f(Dual(1.5, 1.0))
print(y.a, y.b)                        # f(1.5) and f'(1.5)
Output
1.375 4.75

These are f(1.5)=1.375f(1.5) = 1.375f(1.5)=1.375 and f′(1.5)=3(1.5)2−2=4.75,f'(1.5) = 3(1.5)^2 - 2 = 4.75\mathclose{\text{,}}f′(1.5)=3(1.5)2−2=4.75, exactly. The same function, run on ordinary numbers, gives forward differences:

Python
for h in [1e-1, 1e-4, 1e-8, 1e-12]:
    print(f"h = {h:g}: {(f(1.5 + h) - f(1.5))/h}")
Output
h = 0.1: 5.210000000000008
h = 0.0001: 4.750450010000407
h = 1e-08: 4.749999993336473
h = 1e-12: 4.75042227776612

With h=0.1h = 0.1h=0.1 the truncation error is about 0.46. With h=10−8,h = 10^{-8}\mathclose{\text{,}}h=10−8, about the best step, the error is about 7×10−9;7 \times 10^{-9}\mathclose{\text{;}}7×10−9; at h=10−12h = 10^{-12}h=10−12 rounding errors take over, and the error grows again, to about 4×10−4.4 \times 10^{-4}\mathclose{\text{.}}4×10−4. SymPy, given the formula, differentiates it exactly:

Python
import sympy as sp
x = sp.symbols('x')
fp = sp.diff(x**3 - 2*x + 1, x)
print(fp, '|', fp.subs(x, 1.5))
Output
3*x**2 - 2 | 4.75000000000000

To add the sine, give it its derivative rule; the chain rule then comes free. Here is the derivative of sin⁡(x2)\sin(x^2)sin(x2) at 1, which is 2cos⁡1:2\cos 1\mathclose{\text{:}}2cos1:

Python
import math
def sin(d):                            # sin(a + bε) = sin a + (cos a)·b ε
    return Dual(math.sin(d.a), math.cos(d.a)*d.b)

t = Dual(1.0, 1.0)
print(sin(t*t).b, 2*math.cos(1.0))
Output
1.0806046117362795 1.0806046117362795

Automatic differentiation also goes through loops, which a formula does not have. This function squares and adds three times:

Python
def g(x):
    y = x
    for _ in range(3):                 # three times: y becomes y² + x
        y = y*y + x
    return y

print(g(Dual(0.5, 1.0)).b)
print(sp.diff(g(x), x).subs(x, sp.Rational(1, 2)))
Output
9.5
19/2

The program g computes the polynomial ((x2+x)2+x)2+x,\big((x^2 + x)^2 + x\big)^2 + x\mathclose{\text{,}}((x2+x)2+x)2+x, of degree 8, and dual numbers found its derivative at 0.5 without anyone writing that formula down. SymPy agrees: run on the symbol x, the same program builds the formula, which sp.diff then differentiates.

Figure 5.4 compares the methods over the whole range of steps h.h\mathclose{\text{.}}h.

Forwards and backwards

Dual numbers carry derivatives forwards, from the input through each step of the program to the output: this is forward mode automatic differentiation. One run gives the derivative with respect to one input. A neural network, though, has millions of parameters and one number to make small, its error on the training data, and training needs the derivative of that error with respect to every parameter. One forward run per parameter would be far too slow. Backpropagation applies the same chain rule in the other direction: it records the steps of one run, then goes back from the output towards the inputs, multiplying the rates of the steps, and finds all the derivatives in a single backward pass. Backpropagation is the chain rule, organised for many inputs; Module 17 shows how it works.

Watch out

Automatic differentiation differentiates the steps that the program takes, not the function that the programmer had in mind. A program that returns 1 when x=1x = 1x=1 and x⋅xx \cdot xx⋅x otherwise computes x2x^2x2 for every x,x\mathclose{\text{,}}x, but at x=1x = 1x=1 it takes the constant branch, so it reports the derivative 0 there instead of 2.

Exercise 5.4★Rates multiply
  • (a) A bicycle’s pedals turn a front sprocket with 44 teeth; the chain drives a rear sprocket with 11 teeth, fixed to the back wheel, whose circumference is 2.1 m. You pedal at one turn per second. How fast does the bicycle go, in metres per second and in kilometres per hour?
  • (b) Suppose g(2)=5,g(2) = 5\mathclose{\text{,}}g(2)=5, g′(2)=3,g'(2) = 3\mathclose{\text{,}}g′(2)=3, f′(2)=7f'(2) = 7f′(2)=7 and f′(5)=−2.f'(5) = -2\mathclose{\text{.}}f′(5)=−2. Find the derivative of f(g(x))f\big(g(x)\big)f(g(x)) at x=2.x = 2\mathclose{\text{.}}x=2.
Show solution✓ Checked

(a) Three rates multiply. Let ppp and www be the numbers of turns made by the pedals and by the wheel, and sss the distance travelled, in metres. Each turn of the pedals moves 44 links of chain, which turn the rear sprocket, and the wheel, 44/11=444/11 = 444/11=4 times: dw/dp=4.dw/dp = 4\mathclose{\text{.}}dw/dp=4. Each turn of the wheel moves the bicycle 2.1 m: ds/dw=2.1.ds/dw = 2.1\mathclose{\text{.}}ds/dw=2.1. And dp/dt=1dp/dt = 1dp/dt=1 turn per second. So

dsdt=dsdw⋅dwdp⋅dpdt=2.1⋅4⋅1=8.4 m/s.\begin{aligned} \frac{ds}{dt} &= \frac{ds}{dw}\cdot\frac{dw}{dp}\cdot\frac{dp}{dt} \\ &= 2.1 \cdot 4 \cdot 1 = 8.4 \text{ m/s}. \end{aligned}dtds​​=dwds​⋅dpdw​⋅dtdp​=2.1⋅4⋅1=8.4 m/s.​

Exercise 5.10★★★The power rule by induction

A proof by induction shows that a statement holds for every positive integer nnn in two steps. The base case shows it for n=1.n = 1\mathclose{\text{.}}n=1. Then it holds for 1, so for 2, so for 3, and so on for every n,n\mathclose{\text{,}}n, like a row of falling dominoes. (Module 9 uses the method again.)

(a) Base case. For n=1:n = 1\mathclose{\text{:}}n=1: the difference quotient of xxx is (x+h)−xh=1\dfrac{(x + h) - x}{h} = 1h(x+h)−x​=1 for every h≠0,h \ne 0\mathclose{\text{,}}h=0, so ddxx=1=1⋅x0.\dfrac{d}{dx}x = 1 = 1\cdot x^0\mathclose{\text{.}}dxd​x=1=1⋅x0.

Inductive step. Suppose that ddxxn=nxn−1\dfrac{d}{dx}x^n = nx^{n-1}dxd​xn=nxn−1 for some n≥1.n \ge 1\mathclose{\text{.}}n≥1. Then xn+1=x⋅xn,x^{n+1} = x \cdot x^n\mathclose{\text{,}}xn+1=x⋅xn, and by the product rule

ddxxn+1=1⋅xn+x⋅nxn−1=xn+nxn=(n+1)xn,\begin{aligned} \frac{d}{dx}x^{n+1} &= 1 \cdot x^n + x \cdot nx^{n-1} \\ &= x^n + nx^n \\ &= (n + 1)x^n, \end{aligned}dxd​xn+1​=1⋅xn+x⋅nxn−1=xn+nxn=(n+1)xn,​

which is the statement for n+1.n + 1\mathclose{\text{.}}n+1. By induction it holds for every positive integer n.n\mathclose{\text{.}}n.

(b) Base case. For n=1n = 1n=1 the statement says (f1)′=1⋅f′,(f^1)' = 1\cdot f'\mathclose{\text{,}}(f1)′=1⋅f′, which is true.

Inductive step. Suppose that (fn)′=nfn−1f′(f^n)' = nf^{n-1}f'(fn)′=nfn−1f′ at x.x\mathclose{\text{.}}x. Then fn+1=f⋅fn,f^{n+1} = f\cdot f^n\mathclose{\text{,}}fn+1=f⋅fn, and by the product rule

(c) Two methods: __truediv__ for d / e, and __rtruediv__ for a plain number divided by a dual, as in 1/(1 + x*x):

Python
class Dual:
    def __init__(self, a, b=0.0):
        self.a, self.b = a, b
    def __add__(self, other):
        other = other if isinstance(other, Dual) else Dual(other)
        return Dual(self.a + other.a, self.b + other.b)
    def __mul__(self, other):
        other = other if isinstance(other, Dual) else Dual(other)
        return Dual(self.a*other.a, self.a*other.b + self.b*other.a)
    def __truediv__(self, other):            # (a + bε)/(c + dε), with c ≠ 0
        other = other if isinstance(other, Dual) else Dual(other)
        a, b, c, d = self.a, self.b, other.a, other.b
        return Dual(a/c, (b*c - a*d)/c**2)
    def __rtruediv__(self, other):           # number / dual
        return Dual(other)/self
    __radd__, __rmul__ = __add__, __mul__
Python
def f(x):
    return 1/(1 + x*x)

y = f(Dual(2.0, 1.0))
print(y.a, y.b)
